items.clean_ref:
Discharge Summary:
Patient: 45-year-old female
Diagnosis: Multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer that affects the bone marrow

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with multiple purple and dark bruise-like patches on the skin. These patches appeared around the eyes, cheeks, and the front and back of the neck. The areas normally covered by clothing were mostly clear. These skin problems started 2 years ago. Even small bumps or injuries caused these patches to appear. The skin was very easy to damage in most areas. The patient also had several bouts of loose stools and fever over the past 6 months. A physical exam showed the patient was slightly pale and had swelling in both feet. A small sample of skin was taken and tested. It showed a blister-like problem with an abnormal protein buildup called amyloid. Blood tests and a bone marrow test confirmed the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. X-rays and other images of the bones looked normal.

Treatment:
The patient was sent to the blood cancer specialists. Treatment with cancer-fighting drugs was started.

Prognosis:
How well the patient does will depend on how the cancer responds to treatment. It will also depend on how far the cancer has spread. The patient should stay in close contact with the blood cancer care team.

Follow-up:
The patient should see the blood cancer specialists on a regular basis. The patient should also take all medicines as directed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Age: 32
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Hospital: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient came to our hospital with swelling in his right cheek. The swelling had been there for two weeks. Doctors first thought it might be cancer in the mouth area. After a careful exam, doctors found an oval, firm lump about 1 inch by 0.8 inches in size. The lump was located near the right side of the jawbone. An ultrasound of the cheek showed the lump was a fluid-filled sac in the cheek muscle area. There was also some swelling in the tissue around it.

More tests were done, including an MRI scan of the face and neck. The MRI found a small structure inside the sac that looked like a tapeworm head. A small sample was taken from the lump using a thin needle. The sample showed no signs of cancer. X-rays of the chest, both arms, and both thighs were taken. An MRI of the head and eye area was also done. These tests showed no other problem areas in the body.

The patient was told to take pain medicine and medicine to reduce swelling for seven days. The lump slowly got smaller. Medicine to kill the parasite was also given.

Discharge Medications:
Albendazole

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient had a parasitic infection called cysticercosis. This caused a fluid-filled sac to form in the cheek muscle area.

Follow-Up:
The patient should see his regular doctor for continued check-ups.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has gotten better since coming to the hospital. He is doing well and is ready to go home.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should keep taking his albendazole medicine as directed. He should not use tobacco because it has been linked to this type of infection. He should see his regular doctor for continued check-ups. He should tell his doctor about any new or worrying symptoms.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:

The patient came to the emergency room feeling very weak and not eating well. Her health history includes diabetes, high blood pressure, severe joint pain from worn cartilage, and a recent bladder infection treated with antibiotics.

The physical exam showed she was low on body fluids and had low blood pressure. Blood tests showed high calcium levels, high waste product levels in the blood, and low magnesium levels. The patient was diagnosed with a serious blood infection from a bladder infection and moved to the intensive care unit. She received antibiotics and large amounts of fluids through an IV, which helped her vital signs become stable.

On the third day in the hospital, the patient's calcium level went down after receiving salt water fluids and a hormone medicine called calcitonin. However, the calcium level started going up again after three days of calcitonin treatment. More tests, including a special scan of the chest and belly and a full body bone scan, showed no cancer.

Blood tests showed that the systems controlling calcium and certain hormones were not working well, and low function of the adrenal glands may have caused her high calcium levels.

Treatment with a steroid medicine called hydrocortisone was started on the tenth day in the hospital and brought her calcium levels back to normal. Her weakness and poor appetite got better after that. The patient did not return for follow-up visits, and regular checks of bone strength were recommended.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 61-year-old male with a history of controlled type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and past smoking. He came to the hospital with lower back pain and weight loss.

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to Internal Medicine because of lower back pain and weight loss. A CT scan showed broken bones and a growth near the left side of the spine. Doctors thought it might be cancer. More imaging tests showed a growth near the right lung and another in the upper left lung. There were also small spots that could be from infection or swelling. Doctors took a sample from the growth and found pus. Tests showed it contained tuberculosis bacteria. The patient started treatment with four medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HRZE. The patient also saw specialists for physical medicine and bone care. He received physical therapy to help him recover. After 25 days, the patient left the hospital. He was sent to continue physical therapy and to visit a special clinic for tuberculosis care.

Follow-up: The patient finished two months of treatment with four medicines. He is now taking two medicines to fight tuberculosis, called HR. The growths outside the lungs have gone away completely. A new CT scan of the lower back showed the growth there has gotten smaller.

Diagnosis: Long-term infection with swelling caused by tuberculosis.

Condition at discharge: Stable.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 33-year-old Malaysian male, came to the hospital after having a seizure during sleep. Before coming to the hospital, the patient had symptoms like the flu, no appetite, and muscle aches. When he arrived, he was confused but did not have weakness on one side of his body. After each seizure, the patient was confused for about 30 minutes. During the third seizure, his heart stopped beating for 21 seconds. Doctors put in a device called a pacemaker to keep his heart beating normally.

The patient's brain and nerve exam was mostly normal. He did have jerky eye movements, likely caused by a seizure medicine called phenytoin. Even after getting seizure medicine and adjusting the dose, the patient kept having seizures. He also started having pain on the right side of his head and right ear. He felt tenderness and heard a strange sound in his right ear. This later turned into hearing music that was not real. The patient also had a type of seizure that affects awareness and behavior. These signs pointed to a possible brain infection caused by the herpes virus.

Investigations:
Doctors took fluid from the spine two times. The tests were mostly normal but showed slightly high protein levels. Brain scans with dye were normal. A special scan showed slightly less blood flow on the left side of the brain than the right. A second brain wave test showed something slightly off in the right side of the brain near the ear.

Treatment:
The patient started taking a medicine called acyclovir to fight the virus. After one week, he got much better. The seizures and headaches stopped, but he still heard music that was not real for a few more days. The patient left the hospital to finish three weeks of acyclovir at home. When doctors tried to lower the seizure medicine, the seizures came back. So the patient is still taking two seizure medicines called levetiracetam and phenytoin.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with a possible brain infection caused by the herpes virus. The infection was treated well with acyclovir. The patient left the hospital with orders to finish all the medicine and keep taking the seizure medicines.

Diagnosis: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI), a condition where the body makes too much insulin, causing low blood sugar
Treatment: Diazoxide, Octreotide, Lanreotide

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient with CHI came to the children's hospital unit for a planned stay. The goal was to find a different medicine because diazoxide was causing unwanted hair growth.
The care team slowly lowered and then stopped diazoxide for 72 hours to see what would happen. However, this caused repeated episodes of low blood sugar with symptoms.
Octreotide was then started as a shot under the skin four times a day. This medicine helps control blood sugar.
The patient responded well to this dose. She was able to go without food for 24 hours with no low blood sugar.
Lanreotide was then started as a shot under the skin, 30 mg once a month. This is a long-acting medicine similar to octreotide. Octreotide was slowly lowered and then stopped.
A device that checks blood sugar all the time showed good blood sugar control after starting lanreotide. There were no episodes of low blood sugar.
The patient started having repeated low blood sugar episodes with symptoms after starting fluoxetine. Fluoxetine was stopped and the low blood sugar episodes went away within a week.
Two weeks after stopping fluoxetine, the patient's sad mood slowly got better over time with the help of talk therapy.

Final Diagnosis:
Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)

Follow-up Plan:
No further specific follow-up needed at this time.

Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 50-year-old female patient who came to our department with swelling inside the mouth on the left side of the lower jaw for six months. The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The patient was asleep under general anesthesia during the procedure.

History of Present Illness: The patient came to our department with swelling and pain in the left lower jaw area for six months. The swelling grew quickly after the patient had back teeth removed on the lower left side. The patient did not have a fever or trouble swallowing.

Physical Examination: When looking at the outside of the face, the lower left side looked uneven compared to the right side. There were no swollen lymph nodes in the area. When looking inside the mouth, there was a growing mass that spread from front to back and side to side. It went from the area of the first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. The mass measured about 6 by 4 centimeters. The skin covering the mass looked normal in color and feel.

Diagnostic Tests: A panoramic jaw x-ray showed a clear dark area going from the lower left first small back tooth to the area behind the last molar. CT scans, which are detailed pictures of the inside of the body, showed the growth was breaking down bone in the lower left jaw. This bone loss went from the small back teeth area into the back part of the jawbone. A small tissue sample was taken and looked at under a microscope. This test confirmed the growth was an aggressive central giant cell granuloma, which is a type of noncancerous but fast-growing jaw tumor.

Hospital Course: The patient had surgery to remove the growth and rebuild the area using skin and tissue from under the chin. The surgery was done from both outside and inside the mouth to remove all of the growth. The patient went home without any problems.

Follow-up: At checkup visits over the next year, there were no signs that the growth came back. This was checked by looking in the mouth and taking x-rays. The area under the chin where tissue was taken healed well with very little scarring. The small scar is not in a part of the face that people easily see.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 4-month-old baby girl. She was brought to the hospital because she was not making eye contact. She was born 5 weeks early at 35 weeks of pregnancy. There were no known health problems in the family. The patient was found to have Leber congenital amaurosis, also called LCA. This is a rare eye condition that causes severe vision loss. The doctors found this because her eyes turned inward and moved back and forth on their own. A test that checks how the back of the eye responds to light showed no response in both eyes. The patient also had trouble focusing her eyes, which was treated. The doctors did several exams. They looked at the front and back of her eyes. They also checked her whole body for problems with her organs or body chemistry. These tests were normal except for the eye problems already mentioned.

The doctors did many tests to find the cause. They did genetic testing to look for changes in certain genes. These tests did not find any problems. A brain scan called an MRI was done. It showed extra fluid in the spaces around the front parts of the brain. It also showed that a thin wall in the middle of the brain was missing. This wall is called the septum pellucidum. No other brain problems were found. The main connection between the two sides of the brain looked normal. The protective covering around nerves in the brain was developing normally. Later brain scans still showed the missing wall in the middle of the brain. The extra fluid around the brain stayed the same and did not get worse. The doctors thought about a condition called septo-optic dysplasia. However, the eye nerves looked normal and the hormone gland at the base of the brain worked normally. This made the doctors unsure about that diagnosis.

Medical History:
The patient had no other health problems. Her only issues were the eye condition called LCA and the brain scan findings with extra fluid around the brain.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 65-year-old female with a history of thyroid disease was admitted to the hospital. She had been feeling tired and sick to her stomach for one week. She had no history of mental health problems. Her blood tests showed low sodium levels. Her heart test showed some unusual patterns.

Course:
After admission, the patient became more alert at first. Four days later, she started seeing things that were not there. She also became very suspicious of others. She was confused and restless. Mental health doctors were called to help. They gave her a medicine called quetiapine to help calm her confusion. On the same day, she felt sick to her stomach again. She became pale and started sweating. Doctors thought her heart might be failing. They did an emergency heart procedure to check her blood vessels. They found she had a heart condition called broken heart syndrome. This is a type of heart problem often caused by stress. Doctors gave her a steroid medicine called hydrocortisone. Within 3 days, her sodium levels and confusion got much better. A heart imaging test was done 10 days after starting the steroid. It showed her heart was pumping much better than before.

Diagnosis:
Blood tests showed her body was not making enough of certain stress hormones. These hormones are called cortisol and ACTH. Her urine tests also showed low levels of cortisol. Doctors found the patient had a rare condition. Her body could not make enough ACTH hormone. A brain scan was done to check the gland that makes this hormone. The scan showed no growths or problems in that area.

Discharge:
The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep taking hydrocortisone by mouth. She was told to see her regular doctor for follow-up care. She was also told to see a hormone specialist to manage her ACTH hormone problem.

The patient came to our hospital after having trouble urinating for 6 months. The patient also had a small growth at the opening where urine comes out. The patient handled the surgery well and had no problems afterward.

Outcome:
The final lab report showed a very small spot (3 millimeters) of remaining skin cancer. This time, no cancer cells were found at the edges. Now, one year after surgery, the patient shows no signs of cancer.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient will need long-term checkups with regular tests and scans to watch for any return of the cancer. The patient must use a thin tube to empty the bladder on a regular schedule. The patient can control when to empty the bladder. The patient should see a cancer doctor and a bladder doctor for ongoing care and checkups.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:

The patient is a 50-year-old male with an itchy patch of skin on his left hand. He was admitted to the skin care department for evaluation. The patch started as a small, red bump. It slowly grew larger over several months and became a bigger, flaky patch. The patient also had itching and a tingling feeling. Skin cream with steroids helped for a short time, but the patch did not go away. A small tissue sample was taken because the patch looked unusual. The test showed a type of skin swelling called nummular dermatitis. Stronger steroid creams only made the patch flatten for a short time.

Several months later, the patient came back. The center of the patch had become an open sore. He also had lumps under the skin in a line from his left pinky finger up to his elbow. Testing a tissue sample found fish-tank granuloma, an infection caused by a germ called M. marinum. The patient said he had a salt-water fish tank at home. Several of his fish had died weeks after his skin problems started, but the fish were not tested.

Lab tests showed which medicines could kill the germ and which could not. The germ could be killed by amikacin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, rifabutin, and rifampin. The germ could not be killed by ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Treatment with doxycycline and azithromycin did not help after 3 months. The medicines were changed to moxifloxacin and clarithromycin. The patient also put a reusable heat pack on the affected skin for several hours each day. The patient was sent to a surgeon to remove the lumps under the skin on his left hand, wrist, and arm. After 3 months on the new medicines and removal of the lumps, the open sore healed. The removed lumps did not come back.

The patient stayed in the hospital for 17 months until the disease was fully gone. The patient was sent home after tests showed the disease had cleared up. No further medical visits are needed.

This patient was admitted to our facility for severe itching on her right arm. This problem had been going on for six months. She also had weakness in her right arm.

The patient has a known history of multiple myeloma. This is a type of blood cancer.

A CT scan of the neck, an MRI, and a nerve test of the shoulder and arm area were performed. These tests showed a bulging disc in the right side of the neck. The patient was treated with methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1%. This is a steroid cream. She also took hydroxyzine 25mg by mouth every 8 hours. This helped only a little with the itching. Gabapentin was added at 900mg per day. After three months, this medicine controlled the itching well.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS

The patient was sent to see a brain and spine surgeon. She was also sent to see a cancer doctor for more treatment advice.

SUMMARY

The patient had nerve damage in the shoulder and arm area. This was caused by the spread of her blood cancer. The treatment plan included methylprednisolone aceponate cream 0.1% and hydroxyzine 25mg by mouth every 8 hours. Gabapentin at 900mg per day was also added. The patient was sent to a brain and spine surgeon and a cancer doctor for more care.

The patient is a 50-year-old male farmer who was sent to our hospital for emergency care. The patient came in with stomach pain that came and went. Two days before, he had surgery at another hospital to fix a hole in his small intestine and treat an infection that had spread in his belly.

When the patient first went to the other hospital, his kidneys were not working well. He had low potassium levels in his blood. He also had bad belly pain and was making very little urine for 5 days. After surgery, the patient had swelling in his face and trouble breathing. He also had too much acid in his blood, low blood pressure, confusion, and fever. The patient was put on a breathing machine and given medicines to fight infection. These medicines included aztreonam and metronidazole given through a vein. Even with all this care, the patient got worse.

Blood tests showed the patient had a low red blood cell count with some oddly shaped cells. Other test results showed the following. The patient had too many white blood cells and not enough cells that help blood clot. Tests that show swelling in the body were high. Kidney function tests showed the kidneys were not working well. Salt and potassium levels in the blood were too high. Liver tests were also high. An imaging test of the belly showed mild kidney disease and a small fluid buildup near the spleen. It also showed swollen tubes in the liver. A urine test showed a small number of cells that fight infection. A test of fluid from the belly showed some cells that fight infection along with yeast and fungus. A blood test for germs came back clean after 24 hours.

A test of belly fluid found a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. Based on these tests, the infection was treated using standard medical care. Even with treatment, the patient kept getting worse. He was then sent here for emergency care.

Given how sick the patient is, he will keep getting care to support his body. More treatment will be given as needed.

The patient was found to have an infection caused by a fungus called Trichosporon beigelii. This was treated during his hospital stay.

The patient will keep getting follow-up care to make sure he gets the treatment he needs. Instructions for follow-up care will be given at future visits.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 29-year-old woman. She was admitted to the hospital 21 weeks after giving birth. She had diarrhea with blood and stomach pain. A test using a camera to look inside the large intestine was done. It showed swelling and irritation from the rectum to part of the colon. There were also many yellow-white spots. These findings matched a bowel disease called ulcerative colitis. The patient was given a medicine called sulfasalazine. Her symptoms got better. She left the hospital after 2 weeks. During this time, she was given meals based mostly on plants, eggs, and dairy. She also received teaching about eating a plant-based diet. A camera test of the large intestine was done at the end of the stay. It showed the bowel disease was no longer active. The patient's mesalazine dose was slowly lowered to 0.4 grams per day when she left.

During a talk and survey about lifestyle and eating habits, the patient shared some information. She said her diet changed after having her baby. She stayed at her parents' home for about 3 months after delivery. Her mother made traditional Japanese meals as suggested by the midwife. After going back to her own home, the patient said she ate less healthy foods. She also had trouble with bowel movements and upper stomach discomfort. Her eating habits were measured using a plant-based diet score.

Outcome:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition. She was told to keep eating a plant-based diet. The patient stopped taking her medicine 3 weeks after leaving the hospital. She has stayed well without medicine up to now.

The patient went to a skin doctor with red patches and scabbed sores on the scalp that had been there for one month. The first diagnosis was a long-lasting open sore caused by an infection. Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Reason for Admission: Shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient came to the emergency room with shortness of breath that was getting worse. Doctors found a large growth on her thyroid gland. This growth was pressing on her windpipe and making it hard to breathe. The patient was moved quickly to the intensive care unit. There, doctors placed a breathing tube to help her breathe. Brain and chest scans showed the thyroid growth was very large and reaching into the upper chest area. Doctors removed the thyroid gland in surgery 48 hours after the patient arrived. Before waking the patient fully, doctors tested the windpipe. They found the windpipe walls were weak and floppy. The breathing tube stayed in place for 24 hours. It was removed the next day without any problems.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received a steroid medicine called dexamethasone before surgery. She took 12 mg per day for two days. This helped her baby's lungs develop faster. The surgery went well. Doctors did not need to make an opening in her windpipe. After surgery, the patient started taking thyroid hormone pills. The medicine is levothyroxin sodium tablets at 75 mcg per day.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient left the hospital five days after surgery with no problems. Lab tests on the removed tissue showed a thyroid growth with many lumps. Some cells were growing in an unusual way. However, there was no cancer. The patient gave birth to a healthy baby four weeks later.

Recommendations:
The patient should keep taking levothyroxin sodium tablets at 75 mcg per day as directed. She should see her regular doctor for checkups. The doctor will monitor how well her thyroid medicine is working. The doctor will also watch for any problems from the thyroid removal surgery.

Hospital Course:

A 30-year-old man came to the hospital with a fever. He was moved from another hospital in Yunnan Province. Seven days before coming to this hospital, he had surgery to remove his appendix. The doctors found his appendix was badly infected. When he arrived, his body temperature was high at 39.5 degrees Celsius. His blood pressure was 108 over 78, which was normal. The rest of his body check was normal. Blood tests showed his white blood cell count was high. This means his body was fighting an infection. Another blood test called procalcitonin was also high. This test helps find serious infections. A special scan of his belly area was done using dye and x-rays. The scan showed a pocket of infection near where his appendix was removed. The pocket was about 2.3 cm by 2.9 cm in size. The doctors gave him an antibiotic medicine through a vein. The medicine was called moxifloxacin. They started this medicine before they knew exactly what germ was causing the infection.

Management and Treatment:

On Day 3, blood tests found a type of bacteria in his blood. The bacteria was called E. Lenta. The doctors then changed his medicine to one that works better against this germ. The patient received a strong antibiotic called meropenem through a vein. He got 1 gram of this medicine every 8 hours. The patient got better quickly with this treatment. The doctors did not need to drain the infection pocket with a needle or surgery. His fever went away. His blood test numbers went back to normal. He did not need any surgery.

Discharge Plan:

On Day 5, new blood tests showed no germs in his blood. On Day 10, a sound wave test of his belly area was normal. The patient kept getting the meropenem medicine through a vein for 6 more days. The patient got better and left the hospital. The patient has appointments set up to check on his healing. These visits will make sure he fully recovers.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 53-year-old male nurse found to have hepatitis C virus infection

Hospital Course:
In January 2011, the patient was seen at the Outpatient Infectious Diseases clinic because of abnormal liver test results. His hepatitis C virus level was 660,000 units per milliliter, type 3a. A small sample of liver tissue showed ongoing liver swelling with moderate damage and mild to moderate scarring. The patient was a good fit for treatment and began taking two medicines called PEG-IFN-α-2a and ribavirin in March 2011. The patient handled the treatment well. The virus was no longer found in the blood by week four. It stayed gone during the full 24 weeks of treatment. Liver test results returned to normal within the first 3 weeks. The patient had follow-up visits until September 2012. A new liver tissue sample showed less damage and less scarring than before.

Hospitalization:
Nine weeks after finishing the antiviral treatment, the patient developed joint swelling on both sides of the body. The patient had pain and swelling in the wrists, knees, shoulders, and finger joints. The patient also had stiffness in the morning that lasted a long time. An MRI scan showed bone damage and bone thinning near the joints in the wrist, knee, and hand. These findings led to a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, a disease where the body attacks its own joints. Blood tests for rheumatoid factor and another marker for this disease were both positive.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with prednisone, a steroid, and pain relievers for two months. After that, the patient took methotrexate and sulfasalazine. The patient responded quickly and well to this treatment.

Discharge:
The patient went home in good condition with prescriptions for methotrexate and sulfasalazine. The patient should follow up with a joint specialist and a stomach and liver specialist.

The patient is a 70-year-old male with a joint disease called rheumatoid arthritis. He came to the hospital because he had trouble breathing and was coughing up mucus. His joint disease had been well controlled with no joint pain or swelling before this visit. This meant his joint disease was not very active. Blood tests showed high levels of certain markers that point to swelling in the body. Tests also showed the patient had a past infection with a common virus called Epstein-Barr virus.

A scan of the chest showed lung swelling in the lower parts of both lungs with several small round spots. A test of the mucus coughed up from the lungs showed unusual immune cells that looked abnormal. A small piece of lung tissue was removed and tested. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45 years
Sex: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 7 days

Admitting Diagnosis:
A rare type of cancer made of long, thin cells affecting the pancreas

Hospital Course:
The patient was rushed to the hospital because of sudden, severe belly pain and collapse. Doctors found the patient had lost a large amount of blood and was in shock. The belly was swollen and painful to touch. The patient was given blood transfusions and fluids through a vein right away. Blood tests showed very low blood levels at 5g/dl. Imaging tests showed fluid in the belly and a growth near the upper part of the pancreas. Doctors then did emergency surgery to open the belly and find the bleeding. The bleeding came from a growth behind the pancreas that had burst through the lower edge of the pancreas. A tissue sample was taken and tested. The test showed a cancer made of bundles of long, thin cells. This cancer was diagnosed as a rare type called spindle cell sarcoma. The growth was removed during surgery.

Treatment:
The patient stayed in the intensive care unit for 4 days. The patient then received two cancer-fighting drugs called Ifosfamide and Doxorubicin for 6 months after surgery. Before starting these drugs, a special scan with dye was done. The scan showed a growth measuring about 7 by 4.8 by 4.9 centimeters with thin walls attached to the lower edge of the pancreas. The cancer had not spread to other parts of the body.

Outcome:
The patient got better after surgery and left the hospital 7 days after being admitted. The patient was sent to a cancer specialist. Doctors offered surgery to remove the pancreas and the growth. The patient said no to this surgery. The patient received six months of cancer-fighting drugs. The patient died from the disease 18 months after first coming to the hospital.

Summary:
The patient came to the hospital with a rare cancer affecting the pancreas. The cancer was treated with surgery and cancer-fighting drugs given after surgery. The patient left the hospital after staying for 7 days. The patient died from the disease 18 months later.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old girl, was admitted because of vision loss in the right eye for 5 years. She also had headache and vomiting for 6 months. During the exam, the right eye could not see any light at all. The left eye had normal vision. A brain scan showed a fluid-filled sac on the right side of the brain. It measured about 8 by 9 by 6.5 centimeters. A small round lump was seen on the inner side of this sac, near the brain's fluid spaces. Doctors first thought it might be a type of brain tumor. Blood tests later showed that the thyroid gland was not working well due to a problem with hormone signals from the brain.

Treatment:
The patient had surgery to open the skull on the right side of the head. The surgeon drained the fluid-filled sac and created an opening so fluid would not build up again. The fluid inside was yellow and looked like thick oil. It contained fatty crystals and small bits, mostly on the inner side. Lab tests of the tissue showed the sac was a harmless cyst that had become swollen and irritated. The cyst wall was lined with flat to layered skin-like cells. It also had swollen blood vessels and signs of long-term irritation, including certain white blood cells grouped together.

Outcomes:
After surgery, the patient recovered without any problems. The headache and vomiting went away completely. The patient continues to see the doctor regularly. A brain scan done 6 months after surgery showed the cyst has not come back.

Discharge Summary:

The patient is a 43-year-old white male who was generally healthy before this illness. He was admitted to the hospital because of ongoing fever, belly pain, back chest pain, and ear pain. He was found to have an outer ear infection and sent home with amoxicillin-clavulanate and paracetamol, both taken by mouth. Blood tests at that time showed higher than normal levels of CRP, a marker of swelling in the body, and ALT, a liver enzyme.

After leaving the hospital, the patient came back with dark urine, pale stool, and yellow skin and eyes. Swollen lymph nodes were found on both sides of the neck. No other problems were found during the physical exam, chest X-ray, or belly ultrasound.

The patient's blood tests showed a rise in white blood cells, a mild rise in lipase, a digestive enzyme, and higher bilirubin levels. He was given two strong antibiotics called Piperacillin-Tazobactam and Tigecycline. However, his condition got worse. Several of his organs began to fail, and he was moved to the intensive care unit. Tests for immune system problems and immune cell levels came back normal. A liver tissue sample showed damaged liver tissue with changes in structure, scarring, and signs of swelling caused by certain white blood cells. The patient was then started on steroid medicines. This helped improve his condition. His liver function and signs of swelling in the body also got better.

The patient was sent home after 40 days in the hospital. He was given steroid medicine with the dose slowly going down over time. On day 47 after leaving the hospital, he had a heart scan using a special X-ray with dye. The results were normal. Eighteen months later, the patient had no symptoms at all.

The scan also showed the cancer had spread to her lungs and behind her left shoulder blade.

From March to August 2017, the patient joined a research study testing a drug called anlotinib. This study compared the drug to a sugar pill with no medicine in it. The patient got the sugar pill at first. Her cancer got worse during this time.

In September 2017, the patient started taking the real anlotinib drug. Doctors checked her scans every two treatment rounds for the first 12 rounds. After that, they checked every four rounds. The treated tumors were under the muscle on the right side of her neck and behind her left shoulder blade. Other tumors in her neck and lungs were not treated.

The patient took anlotinib for 52 treatment rounds in total. The treated tumors shrank by almost 94 percent. No new tumors appeared. The patient had some side effects during the study. These included high blood pressure, fast heartbeat, twitching in hands and feet, loose stools, skin problems on hands and feet, and headaches. Most side effects were mild to moderate. Most were controlled with medicine.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient came to the clinic at 34 weeks and 1 day of pregnancy. She came to have a large growth in the vagina and sores on the outer genital area checked. An ultrasound done through the vagina showed swollen veins in the vaginal wall. The patient had a small tissue sample taken. The sample showed normal vaginal skin with some changes from irritation. Her pregnancy history included 2 past deliveries by surgery through the belly, 1 pregnancy that grew outside the womb, and pregnancy-related high blood sugar controlled by diet. The patient said she had yellow discharge from the vagina, pain when urinating, and discomfort that got worse when walking. She had tried a yeast infection medicine before, but it did not help her pain. A detailed check of the baby at 26 weeks and 2 days showed mild swelling in both of the baby's kidneys.

During the physical exam, groups of soft swollen veins were seen on the front and side walls of the vagina. These swollen veins filled the vagina and stuck out past the vaginal opening. Another doctor looked at the patient and agreed she had large swollen veins in the vagina. The patient was sent back to her regular doctor for ongoing pregnancy care.

RECOMMENDATIONS:

The patient was told she should have another surgical delivery through the belly. This was because of her past surgical deliveries and the risk of heavy bleeding if she tried to deliver through the vagina. The patient was also told to see her regular doctor for ongoing pregnancy care.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:

Swollen veins in the vagina

DISCHARGE PLAN:

The patient was sent home and told to continue pregnancy care with her regular doctor. No other tests were done to check for swollen veins in the food pipe or blood flow tests of the arms and legs. As often happens with swollen veins in the genital area, the patient's swollen vaginal veins went away completely by her checkup 6 weeks after giving birth.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:

None

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient is told to see her regular doctor for ongoing pregnancy care.

FOLLOW-UP:

The patient is told to see her regular doctor for ongoing pregnancy care.

items.clean_ref:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 84 years
Sex: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient came to the ear, nose, and throat clinic with a growth on the scalp. The growth had been getting bigger for 2 months after a skin cancer removal surgery. A tissue sample showed a type of skin cancer that had spread deeper into the skin. The skin also showed severe sun damage. The doctors removed the cancer through surgery. This left an open wound about 5 by 7 centimeters in size. The wound went down to the tough tissue covering the skull. The doctors talked about ways to help the wound heal. They chose to use a special skin graft material called vCPM. The vCPM was placed directly on the wound and covered with a non-stick bandage. The patient came back to the clinic 7 days after the first treatment. A second piece of vCPM was placed on the wound, which now had healthy new tissue growing. The patient returned on day 14. The wound had shrunk to about 3 by 5 centimeters. New skin was growing well over the wound. The doctors decided a third treatment was not needed. At the day 21 visit, the wound had fully closed with very little scarring. Six months after treatment, the wound stayed closed. The redness continued to fade. The patient had no problems and was very happy with the results.

DIAGNOSIS:
Skin cancer that spread deeper into the skin, with severe sun damage to the skin

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient should see the doctor for regular check-ups to watch how the wound heals. The patient should tell the doctor right away about any signs of infection or slow healing.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient has appointments scheduled with the doctor to check on wound healing.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: Not specified
Medical Record Number: Not specified

Admission Date: Not specified
Discharge Date: Not specified

Admitting Diagnosis: Wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula

Hospital Course: The 73-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with decreased vision and wavy or distorted vision for 6 months in her left eye. Initial examination showed the sharpest vision with glasses was 20/80 in the left eye and 20/25 in the right eye. A detailed eye exam showed wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula. A special imaging scan of the retina confirmed a hole going all the way through the macula with attached edges. It also showed a partly detached gel layer on top of the raised blister. Treatment with eye injections to stop abnormal blood vessel growth was started. The patient received three monthly injections of bevacizumab (1.25 mg) into the eye. After 4 weeks, the first injection made the fluid-filled blister go away and brought the edges of the hole closer together. However, vision got worse to 20/160. At the follow-up visit, the second injection was given after four weeks. The imaging scan showed the hole had closed completely and vision improved greatly to 20/50. During later follow-up visits, the fluid-filled blister came back, but the hole in the macula stayed closed. Ongoing eye injections with bevacizumab given as needed made the blister go away and kept vision stable.

Discharge Diagnosis: Wet age-related macular degeneration with a fluid-filled blister under the center of the retina and a related hole in the macula

Discharge Education: The patient was told about the importance of continued eye checkups and taking medication as directed. The possible side effects of the medication were explained. The patient was also told to report any new symptoms right away.

Follow-Up Care: The patient will follow-up with her eye doctor in three months.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Medical History:
The patient was a 26-year-old female who had been told she had colon cancer six years earlier. The patient came to the hospital for a regular checkup.

Hospital Course:
During the exam, the patient had no health concerns and no visible signs of illness. More tests were done, including a special scan using dye called a CCT scan. This scan found a growth near the center of the chest. The growth had smooth edges and looked the same throughout. Several swollen lymph nodes were also found in the chest area. The patient then had a PET/CT scan. This scan uses a small amount of a sugar-like substance to find active cells in the body. The scan showed the growth was slightly more active than normal tissue. The patient also had an MRI scan of the chest area. This scan uses magnets to create pictures of the inside of the body. The MRI showed a growth that looked a certain way on different types of images. Based on the scan results and the patient's health history, doctors thought the growth could be one of several things. These included cancer that spread from another part of the body, lung cancer, a blood cancer called lymphoma, or a condition called sarcoidosis.

Results:
Blood tests showed that the patient had a high level of a protein called IgG4. The level was 723, which is much higher than the normal level of 135.

Diagnosis:
Doctors did surgery to take a small piece of lung tissue to test. The test showed the patient had a disease called IgG4-related lung disease. This is a condition where the immune system causes swelling in the lungs.

Condition at Discharge:
When the patient left the hospital, the patient was in stable condition. The patient was given information about the diagnosis. The patient was told to see their regular doctor for ongoing care.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient should see their regular doctor for continued checkups and care of this condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 5-year-old Chinese girl, came to the emergency room with cough, fever, headache, vomiting, and unusual behavior with her parents. She was placed in the children's intensive care unit. Doctors found she had a serious blood infection and a lung infection. She received antibiotics to fight infection, medicine to boost her immune system, and limited fluids. The patient got worse and fell into a deep sleep state where she could not wake up. Her blood pressure dropped too low. Her heart beat in an uneven pattern and her oxygen levels fell too low. A heart test showed her heart's electrical signals were too slow. Blood tests showed she had an underactive thyroid gland that was never treated. This was caused by her own immune system attacking her thyroid gland. Doctors quickly started giving her thyroid medicine called levothyroxine through a tube in her nose to her stomach. She also received medicine to raise her blood pressure, a machine to help her breathe, and a machine to help clean her blood like her kidneys would. Two days after starting the thyroid medicine, she woke up and her body temperature went back to normal. The breathing tube was removed on the fifth day after starting the thyroid medicine. Her thyroid medicine dose was lowered before she went home. She left the hospital taking thyroid medicine once a day at a dose of 3 micrograms per kilogram per day.

Patient: 20-year-old Japanese woman with intellectual disability and seizure disorder

History and Physical Examination:
The patient came in with pain in her lower belly. Doctors found a growth with many fluid-filled sacs in her pelvic area. A special scan showed that both of her ovaries were swollen. BMPM, a rare and fast-growing tumor

Nine months after the second surgery, the tumor has not come back.

The patient came to our hospital because of long-term sinus problems. Since the age of 11, the patient had several serious allergic reactions during surgeries and eye exams. These reactions happened when doctors gave medicine to make him sleep. The patient and his family were very scared to go to hospitals for 10 years. This fear started after his last serious allergic reaction at age 29 during eye removal surgery.

An allergy doctor checked the patient. The doctor did skin tests for morphine and ketamine using standard amounts. The first tests showed no allergy. We told the patient to never use ketamine or morphine for future surgeries. We updated the patient's drug allergy card. We tested other drugs that could be used instead. Those drugs did not cause a reaction. Doctors used these safe drugs for the patient's sinus surgery. The surgery went well with no allergic reactions.

The patient was told to watch carefully for allergy signs if given other sleep medicines in the future. The patient understood all the instructions. The patient went home feeling well. We gave the patient and his caregivers a full report about this hospital stay.

Discharge Medications:

None recommended.

Follow-up:

The patient should see the allergy doctor if needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
DOB: [redacted]
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Attending Physician: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: West syndrome (a type of seizure disorder in infants)

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 2-month-old baby boy. He had heart surgery before this hospital stay to fix a hole between the lower chambers of his heart. He came to the hospital because he was crying a lot and could not be calmed. During these episodes, his neck would stretch back. His arms and body would become stiff. Sometimes he would swallow and throw up afterward. Doctors first thought the problem was acid reflux. They started medicine for acid reflux, but it did not help.

Over the next few weeks, the episodes happened more often and got worse. The patient's mother recorded a video of one episode. The video showed the patient having bending spasms. The patient then had surgery to help stop acid from coming back up. This surgery did not help either. The symptoms kept happening. The patient also had arm spasms during episodes. These signs finally pointed to West syndrome.

A brain wave test confirmed West syndrome. A brain scan showed no problems. The right treatment started when the patient was 8 months old. By then, there were already signs of developmental delays. West syndrome is rare. Doctors suspected it based on the patient's age and medical history after a full brain and nerve exam.

This is the first known case where West syndrome was mistaken for acid reflux. Focusing too much on acid reflux in children may cause doctors to miss other conditions. Doctors should consider acid reflux mainly in children at higher risk. This includes children with brain conditions that affect movement. It also includes children who had surgery for problems with their food pipe. Acid reflux should also be considered when symptoms clearly point to it. These symptoms include throwing up blood or long-term vomiting with poor growth.

Discharge Diagnosis: West syndrome (a type of seizure disorder in infants)

Final Condition at Discharge:
When the patient left the hospital, he still had symptoms of West syndrome. The right treatment had been started. The family was told to see the children's doctors. They will help manage medicines and do more tests.

Discharge Medications:
Not Applicable

Follow-Up:
The parents were told to see a children's doctor for regular checkups. They should watch the patient's condition closely. The patient also has appointments with a brain and nerve doctor for more tests and care.

Hospital Course: A 73-year-old male patient came to the hospital with very high blood pressure after heart bypass surgery. The patient had a history of type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, heart disease, prostate cancer, and high blood pressure that had been harder to control over the past 2 years. The patient's family history was normal, except for some sudden deaths among relatives on the mother's side. A CT scan showed a small growth on the right adrenal gland, which sits on top of the kidney. Blood tests showed high levels of certain hormones, with no signs of inherited conditions. A special imaging scan showed a small growth about 2 by 2 by 3 centimeters on the right adrenal gland with no spread to other parts of the body. The patient had surgery to remove the adrenal gland. Tests after surgery confirmed the growth was a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor. The patient has been sent home and will continue care with regular doctor visits.

Summary of Hospital Stay: The patient was admitted because of very high blood pressure after surgery that was hard to control even with medicine. After more tests, doctors confirmed the patient had a pheochromocytoma, a type of tumor. The patient had surgery to remove the adrenal gland, and there were no problems during the procedure. The patient has been sent home and will see doctors at regular office visits.

Diagnosis: Pheochromocytoma is a tumor that grows in the adrenal gland. It makes the body produce too many stress hormones. This can cause high blood pressure, fast or pounding heartbeat, headaches, sweating, and blurry vision.

Treatment: The patient had surgery to remove the tumor, and there were no problems. The patient will keep taking medicine and making healthy lifestyle changes to manage ongoing health issues. These include diabetes, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure.

Prognosis: How well the patient does depends on the size of the tumor, whether it is cancerous, and other health problems. In this case, the growth was small. Lab tests showed the tumor cells were growing very slowly. Because of this, the patient's outlook is good.

Follow-up: The patient has been sent home and will return for regular doctor visits. These visits will help manage ongoing health issues and check if the tumor comes back or spreads. The patient will have blood and urine tests to check hormone levels and track recovery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 51-year-old female

Admission Date: February 2013

Discharge Date: October 2015

Diagnosis: Returning jaw tumor (ameloblastoma)

Procedure: Surgery to remove part of the right lower jawbone and rebuild it using bone from the hip, followed by placing dental implants and a permanent set of replacement teeth

Hospital Course:

The patient came to the department in February 2013 because of pain in the lower jaw. She had a jaw tumor that kept coming back and had several surgeries before to drain it. The patient was not happy with her care at the other hospital and came to our department to have the tumor fully removed. After a complete checkup, we planned to remove all of the tumor and rebuild the jaw right away using bone from the hip. In March 2013, the patient had surgery to remove part of the right lower jawbone (teeth 43 to 46, about 35 mm long). The care team watched closely to make sure the tumor did not come back. Follow-up visits showed no signs of the tumor returning, but the patient still had trouble chewing on the right side. Because of this, we suggested a permanent set of replacement teeth. In November 2014, the metal plate was taken out of the new bone, and four dental implants were placed. After that, the patient had surgery to create more space in the mouth for the new teeth. All four implants joined well with the bone. The patient received the final set of permanent replacement teeth in October 2015. The patient has kept good mouth care habits. There are no signs of the tumor coming back or problems with the bone or implants. The patient was sent home in October 2015.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient should keep brushing and cleaning the mouth well and follow the regular care schedule. The patient should come to all follow-up visits so the care team can check for any return of the tumor and make sure the implants stay healthy. If the patient has any worries or questions, the patient should call the department for help.

Curved spine due to wear and tear, with the spine out of line both front-to-back and side-to-side, along with narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back

The patient was admitted with back pain and leg pain in both legs when walking. After testing, she was found to have a curved spine from wear and tear. Discharge Summary

Patient: 22-year-old male

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with muscle loss and shaking in both hands and forearms. These problems started slowly about 5 years ago. Cold weather made the symptoms worse. After looking at all the test results, the doctors found the patient has Hirayama Disease. The patient was treated without surgery.

Diagnosis:

Hospital Course:

The ten-year-old female patient came to the hospital because she had trouble walking and stiffness in both legs for the past six months. During the physical exam, doctors found her muscles were stiff and jerky when moved. All four limbs had higher than normal muscle tightness. Her leg strength was slightly weak. She also had shaking when holding a position and muscle spasms that caused twisting movements. Her reflexes were stronger than normal when tested. Her ability to feel touch, her brain nerve function, and her balance were all normal. The patient was diagnosed with a movement disorder that responds to medicine called dopa-responsive dystonia. Doctors knew this because her symptoms got worse as the day went on. They gave her a test dose of levodopa and carbidopa medicine. Her muscle spasms got much better within two days. She was treated with three medicines called Levodopa, Carbidopa, and Trihexyphenidyl.

Discharge Summary:

The ten-year-old female patient came to the hospital with trouble walking and stiff legs that caused her to fall often. Her muscles were stiff and jerky when moved. She had increased muscle tightness, slight weakness, shaking when holding still, and twisting muscle spasms in all four limbs. Her reflexes were stronger than normal. Her ability to feel touch, brain nerve function, and balance were all normal. The patient was diagnosed with dopa-responsive dystonia. Her symptoms got worse as the day went on. She got much better after taking levodopa and carbidopa medicine. The medicine was continued and the patient kept getting better. A gene test was planned but could not be done because of limited resources. The patient left the hospital in good condition and will come back for a follow-up visit.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]

Date of Admission: [Date of Admission]

Date of Discharge: [Date of Discharge]

Hospitalized for: Narrowing of the Left Arm Artery

Brief Hospital Course:

The patient, a 4-year-old boy, was admitted after doctors heard an unusual heart sound during a checkup. The doctor found that the pulse in the left arm was weak and blood pressure was low in that arm. The pulse in the right arm was normal. The patient was 100 cm tall. The left arm was 10 mm shorter than the right arm.

A heart ultrasound showed the heart structure was normal. However, it showed the main artery to the left arm was in an unusual position with uneven blood flow. A special scan of the blood vessels was done to confirm what was wrong. The scan showed the artery to the left arm was 70-80% blocked near where it starts. Because one arm was shorter than the other, treatment was needed. The patient was scheduled to have a small tube placed inside the artery to open it up.

The procedure went well, and the patient handled it without problems. A small metal tube was placed inside the narrowed part of the artery. Pictures taken after the procedure showed the tube was in the right place. Blood was flowing well through the left arm artery. The patient received blood-thinning medicine through an IV overnight. The patient went home with aspirin to take by mouth.

At check-up visits 3 and 6 months later, the pulse and blood pressure in the left arm were almost normal. The arm length had improved a lot. An ultrasound of the left arm showed smooth blood flow in the artery. The boy has been checked for 4 years now. There is no longer any difference in arm length.

Discharge Diagnosis: Narrowing of the Left Arm Artery.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient will keep taking aspirin as the doctor ordered. Follow-up visits should be scheduled as the doctor instructs. Parents should keep the patient's medical records up to date. Parents should bring these records to each visit.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age/Sex: 29/Female

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Achalasia (a condition where the tube that carries food to the stomach does not work properly)

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 29-year-old female who had trouble swallowing that got worse over time. She came to the hospital because swallowing became very difficult. The patient was told she had achalasia three years ago but chose not to get treatment. About a month before coming to the hospital, her regular doctor gave her iron pills. After taking the pills for three weeks, her swallowing problems became much worse. She was sent to a stomach and digestive system doctor for more tests.

When the patient arrived, she had no pain when swallowing, no upset stomach, and no throwing up. The physical exam showed nothing unusual.

The patient had an X-ray test where she swallowed a special liquid. This showed a widened food tube with a narrowed bottom that looked like a bird's beak. It also showed something stuck in the lower part of the food tube. A camera test was done to look inside the food tube. This showed the food tube was widened. There was an oval-shaped, black mass stuck in the lower part of the food tube. The mass was made of the iron pills that had clumped together. There were no sores inside the food tube. The muscle at the bottom of the food tube was very tight.

The doctors tried to break up the mass and push it into the stomach. They had to stop because the tight muscle made it too risky. There was also a chance food could go into the lungs. The doctors used a small basket tool to pull the mass out instead.

A test was done to measure how well the food tube muscles work. The results matched the diagnosis of achalasia. In a later procedure, the doctors stretched the tight muscle using a balloon. The balloon was about 1.2 inches wide. The procedure worked well.

The patient had no symptoms during the 3 years of check-ups after treatment.

Discharge Condition:

The patient got better after the balloon stretching treatment. The patient left the hospital in good condition. The patient was told to see her stomach and digestive system doctor at her scheduled visits.

Discharge Medications:

None

Follow-up:

The patient was told to see her stomach and digestive system doctor at her scheduled visits.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 79-year-old male with advanced prostate cancer who came to the hospital with a growth on the opening of his penis. A tissue sample showed a type of skin cancer called squamous cell carcinoma. The patient had surgery to remove part of his penis and nearby lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small glands that help fight infection. The surgery found cancer in three out of seven lymph nodes on the right side of his groin. The cancer was staged as T2N2M0, meaning it had spread to nearby lymph nodes but not to other parts of the body. The patient received cancer-killing drugs called carboplatin and paclitaxel at low doses. He also received radiation treatment to the right groin area.

Nine months later, the cancer came back and spread to lymph nodes again. The patient received more cancer-killing drugs and radiation with the goal of curing the cancer. This included another round of low dose carboplatin and paclitaxel. Radiation was given to the left pelvic area. He responded well at first, but the cancer eventually grew again. The doctors then considered a different treatment called atezolizumab. This drug helps the body's defense system fight cancer.

After about two years on atezolizumab, the patient developed a skin condition called bullous pemphigoid. This causes blisters and is a known side effect of this type of drug. The patient was given a steroid medicine called prednisone. His blistering went away quickly.

At the time of this report, the cancer has almost completely gone away. The patient has stopped treatment for now. Follow-up appointments have been scheduled to check on his progress.

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with belly pain and swelling, a high number of white blood cells, and too many allergy-related cells in the blood. Blood tests also showed high levels of a protein linked to allergies. Scans showed a moderate amount of fluid buildup in the belly. Tissue samples showed too many allergy-related cells in the stomach and intestines. This pointed to a condition called eosinophilic gastroenteritis, where allergy cells cause gut inflammation. The patient was given a steroid pill called prednisone by mouth. This helped the symptoms go away. The fluid in the belly and the thickening of the gut walls also went away completely. After finishing the steroid treatment, the patient had no more symptoms. No other treatment was needed.

Hospital Course Summary:
A 28-year-old Saudi female with no major past health problems came in with two weeks of belly pain and swelling. During the physical exam, the doctor found tenderness all over the belly and a moderate amount of fluid buildup. Blood tests showed a high white blood cell count with too many allergy-related cells. A protein linked to allergies was also high. Scans showed moderate fluid in the belly, thickened gut walls, and swollen lymph nodes near the intestines. The patient had a scope test to look at the upper gut and another to look at the lower gut. Tissue samples from these tests confirmed too many allergy-related cells in the gut. This matched a diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

Treatment started with a steroid pill called prednisone by mouth. The patient's symptoms got better. The fluid in the belly and the thickened gut walls went away completely. After finishing the steroid treatment, the patient had no symptoms and did not need more treatment. Follow-up blood tests and scans showed the improvement lasted. The patient was sent home with instructions to see their regular doctor if needed.

Hospital Course:
A 66-year-old female patient came to the gum care department at M. S. Ramaiah Dental College and Hospital in Bangalore. She had a burning feeling in her gums and bleeding gums for the past month.

Medical History:
The patient was not taking any medicines and had no major health problems. She had never had dental treatment before.

Examination Findings:
The dentist looked at the outside of the patient's face and body. The patient had some skin patches on her scalp. She also had a thick, rough patch of skin behind her left ear. The dentist then looked inside the patient's mouth. The gums around the upper and lower front teeth were red. This included the gums at the edges, the gums attached to the teeth, and the gums between the teeth. In some areas, the top layer of gum tissue was peeling off.

Diagnosis:
Based on what the dentist saw and lab test results, the patient likely has discoid lupus erythematosus. This is a condition where the body's defense system attacks its own skin and gum tissue.

Treatment:
The dentist gently cleaned the teeth to remove buildup. This was done carefully to avoid hurting the gums. The patient was told to use a soft toothbrush and rinse with chlorhexidine 0.12 percent mouthwash. The patient was also told to apply triamcinolone acetonide paste inside the mouth two to three times per day. This paste helps reduce soreness and swelling.

Follow-up:
The patient was asked to come back for check-up visits and ongoing care.

items.clean_ref:
Hospital Course:
The patient is a 71-year-old Japanese woman. She had left hip pain for 10 years and swelling in her left leg for 1 year. A physical exam showed she could not move her left hip normally. Her hip could only bend to 80 degrees and had limited movement in other directions. X-rays showed severe joint damage in her left hip. This was caused by a hip problem she was born with. CT scans and MRI scans showed that blood vessels in her leg were being pressed by a growth. This growth was not there 8 years ago on an earlier X-ray. Doctors found that the growth was a piece of bone that had broken off due to the joint damage. The patient had surgery to replace her hip and remove the growth. Right after surgery, the swelling in her left leg went down. Her recovery went smoothly with no problems. At her last check-up, 3 years after surgery, the patient could walk without help. She could do all daily activities on her own. The growth had not come back.

Diagnoses:
Severe joint damage in the left hip caused by a hip problem present since birth.

Procedures performed:
Full hip replacement surgery with removal of the growth. Doctors used a short stem that fits into the thigh bone, a ceramic ball measuring 32mm, and a 48mm socket that attaches without cement. The socket has a plastic lining.

Tissue study findings:
The outer layer was made of cartilage. The center had normal bone tissue. No cancer cells were found.

Discharge condition:
Stable.

Functional status at discharge:
The patient was able to walk on her own and the growth had not come back.

Hospital Course:

The patient came in with a high fever that came and went for three days. He also had bleeding gums and a mild headache. He then became more and more sleepy over time. Tests showed he had a very low platelet count and his red blood cells were breaking apart. The doctors found he had a rare blood disorder called TTP that causes these problems. He was quickly started on a treatment to replace his blood plasma. He also began taking a steroid medicine called prednisolone by mouth.

On the fifth day of being sick, the patient had two seizures where his whole body shook. These seizures then turned into ongoing brain activity problems. He needed to be put on a breathing machine in the intensive care unit. On day 18, he lost strength in both legs and could not control his bladder or bowels. A special scan showed bleeding at several spots along his spine.

The patient had 16 plasma replacement treatments and high doses of steroids. But his platelet count stayed very low. The doctors then looked for other causes. A blood test found high levels of a virus called CMV. He was started on an antiviral medicine called valganciclovir, 450 mg once a day for 21 days. About 6 days after starting this medicine, his platelet count went up. His red blood cells also stopped breaking apart.

The patient's blood tests later returned to normal. The virus was no longer found in his blood. He could walk again with some help. He could also control his bladder and bowels normally again. The patient was moved to a rehab center for more care.

A 72-year-old man came in with a painless lump in his belly that did not bother him. Doctors found a large mass in the middle part of his belly using special scans. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not Disclosed
Gender: Female
Age: 80

Hospital Course:
The patient came in with a slow-growing, painless fluid-filled sac near the outer right eye area. This sac had been there for some time. It caused the eyelid to droop, the eye to bulge forward slightly, and the eye to sit a bit lower than normal. A special scan using magnets (MRI) showed a round growth that did not absorb the contrast dye. Another scan using X-rays (CT) showed changes to the eye socket bones. The bone had worn away near where two skull bones meet. These tests confirmed the growth was a dermoid cyst, a type of harmless sac present from birth. The patient chose not to have surgery to remove the cyst and repair the bone. Instead, the patient had the fluid drained from the cyst several times. After agreeing to treatment, the patient had a procedure to shrink the cyst using a special solution. The first treatment used a numbing medicine mixed with a drug to reduce bleeding. Then pure alcohol was put into the cyst to shrink it. The area was then rinsed with salt water. The patient had two more treatments three months apart. After the last treatment, the cyst became smaller. It stayed small for one year with no signs of growing back. The patient said the loose skin was blocking part of her vision. The doctors did eyelid surgery to remove extra skin. At the same time, they took a small sample of the cyst to study. Lab tests showed the sample contained skin tissue with sweat and oil glands. This confirmed it was a dermoid cyst.

Condition at Discharge:
The treatment to shrink the cyst and the tissue sample test were successful. When the patient left the hospital, there were no signs that the cyst was coming back.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will keep seeing her regular doctor near her home for check-ups. The patient should contact her doctor if any new problems come up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 52-year-old African American woman who has had multiple pregnancies

Diagnosis: Urethral diverticulum (a pouch or sac that forms in the tube that carries urine out of the body)

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted after she fainted. She had heavy vaginal bleeding for 2 days before admission. She was passing large blood clots and had pain in her lower belly. A pelvic exam showed blood clots in the vagina. There was also a raw, damaged area on the vaginal wall near the urine tube. A CT scan (a special X-ray) showed a growth inside the vagina. It also showed a swollen lymph node near the right ovary. On day 2 in the hospital, the patient had a procedure while asleep. Doctors took tissue samples, but the results did not show a clear answer.

During days 3 through 5, the patient's bleeding slowed down a lot. On day 6, doctors did another procedure while the patient was asleep. The tissue samples showed no cancer. Doctors used a special clamp in the urine tube. The urology team (doctors who treat bladder and urine problems) was called in during the procedure. They confirmed the patient had a pouch in the urine tube. The pouch was removed. Doctors then repaired the area in layers around a urine drainage tube.

On day 9 after surgery, the patient came back with bleeding. Some stitches had come loose in the damaged tissue. These were removed. New stitches were placed to close the tissue. The final tissue tests showed the tissue was not cancerous.

Treatment:

Removal of the pouch in the urine tube and repair in layers around a urine drainage tube.

Follow-up:

The patient visited the urology clinic 2 weeks later. A special X-ray test was done to check the urine tube and bladder. It showed no leaking. A physical exam showed the vagina was healing well with no problems.

Disposition:

The patient left the hospital in stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 29-year-old man from Syria. He came to the hospital because of painless swelling in his right testicle. The swelling had been there for 12 months. During the exam, the right testicle was larger than normal but did not hurt when touched. Blood tests were done to check for cancer markers. These tests came back normal. An ultrasound of the scrotum showed a 7-centimeter mass in the right testicle. The mass had low echoes, many blood vessels, and fluid-filled areas. Surgery was done to remove the right testicle through a cut in the groin area. A full body scan showed no cancer spread to the lymph nodes or other parts of the body.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was found to have a rare type of testicular cancer called Sertoli cell sarcoma. There was also a fast-growing cancer that had no specific features. Both cancers were only in the testicle. The tumor had small, medium, and large cells grouped together in sheets. Large areas of dead tissue were also found. Some areas had oddly shaped cells that were dividing quickly. These cells were surrounded by tough, fiber-like tissue. The cancer did not grow through the outer covering of the testicle. The tube that carries sperm and the tissue next to the testicle were not affected. The cancer had not spread into blood vessels or lymph channels.

Treatment:
Tests confirmed the patient had Sertoli cell sarcoma with fast-growing cancer in the testicle only. Doctors strongly recommended additional cancer-killing drug treatment after surgery. However, the patient said no to this treatment and moved to a different area.

Follow-up:
The patient should see a doctor regularly to check if the cancer comes back. The patient should tell a doctor right away about any new symptoms that might be related to the cancer.

Doctors moved these organs back to where they belong. They used a special patch to close the hole in the muscle.

The patient healed well with no problems. The patient left the hospital 10 days after surgery. The patient was told to see their regular doctor for follow-up care. The patient was told to keep taking medicine as directed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Louise
Age: 16
Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), a condition that affects how a person communicates and interacts with others

Hospital Course:
Louise is a 16-year-old girl with autism. Testing showed she thinks and learns at the level of a 13-year-old. Louise grew up in a small country village in Italy with both parents until age nine. Her parents then split up. Her father moved her to Canada. There she went to school and got help from mental health doctors. She also received treatment for a related condition called OCD. OCD causes unwanted repeated thoughts and behaviors.

Over 5 years in Canada, Louise worked with many mental health helpers. She attended school with special changes made to help her learn. Later, a court ordered her to go back to Italy to live with her mother. The court did not find that living with her mother would cause serious harm. However, the mental health doctors disagreed. They believed moving Louise back to Italy could hurt her. The change in her surroundings and less access to mental health care for young people would likely make her symptoms worse.

The mental health doctors also looked into claims that the mother emotionally mistreated Louise. During her time in Italy, Louise was reportedly put down and called hurtful names. The doctors also noted that her OCD could make the move to Italy even harder for her.

The doctors conclude that Louise has a complicated situation because of her condition and history. She needs ongoing medical care and support. The mental health doctors say it is important for Louise to have access to mental health services for young people. She also needs special changes at school to help her learn. These services were available to her in Canada. They should also be available wherever she lives now. The doctors suggest watching her condition closely. They recommend regular visits with medical professionals to check her progress and change her treatment plan if needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Date of Birth: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Admission Diagnosis:
The patient was admitted with a hole in the heart wall, blood vessels connected to the wrong part of the heart, a slow heart rhythm that only beats every other time, slightly blue skin color, and fluid buildup in the lungs.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the conditions listed above. The first exam showed the patient had bluish skin and lower than normal oxygen levels between 85% and 94%. A heart ultrasound done after birth confirmed the blood vessels were connected wrong. It also showed two large veins in the upper body instead of one, a missing large vein in the lower body, and a hole in the wall between the upper heart chambers. The patient had successful heart surgery and received a device to help the heart beat regularly at 9 days old.

Diagnostic Assessments:
A blood test that looks at genes found a small extra copy of part of one chromosome. This copied section contains 11 genes. Seven of these genes are listed in a medical database. Four of them are linked to known health conditions.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient went home at 3 weeks old and was doing well. A checkup at 2 months showed no problems.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient's family learned why regular visits with a children's heart doctor are important. They were told to watch the baby's health at home. This includes checking oxygen levels every day and watching how the baby feeds. The family was also told to keep up with pacemaker checkups and get all vaccines the baby's doctor recommends.

Follow-up:
The patient will have regular visits with the children's heart doctor and regular doctor. These visits will check the heart condition, growth, and development. A visit with a genetics doctor will be suggested to understand how the chromosome change might affect the patient's health over time.

Disposition:
The patient went home in stable condition with improved heart symptoms and a good chance for healthy long-term results.
